$comment: What a budgeted page owes a keyboard and a screen reader before the build refuses it.
THE GAP THIS CLOSES, and it is the twin of .github/perf-budgets.json. The suite here is
strong on WRONG (the unit suite, the mutation drill, the flake drill) and, since the perf
budgets landed, on SLOW. Nothing asked whether the page could still be USED. A change that
drops the `lang` attribute, loses the `<main>` landmark, breaks the skip link, or ships a
control nothing can name is green in `npm run check:ci`, green in the rubric review, and
green in every Playwright spec beside this one — because those specs drive the page by CSS
selector and a selector does not care whether a human could have reached the element.
Under heavy agent authorship these degrade one component at a time, and the first thing
that reports it is somebody using the product with a keyboard.
WHY THERE IS NO axe-core HERE. This repository is deliberately zero-dependency in its gate
layer (ADR-0008), and a11y-rule engines are a large runtime dependency behind rubric A4.
Everything below is evaluated in the page with the DOM APIs the browser already has, which
is why the rule set is SMALL and each rule says exactly what it looks at. It is not an audit
and it does not pretend to be one — `notCovered` is the honest half of this file.
TWO RUNGS, the same discipline as everything else here (docs/adr/0007-gate-rung-discipline.md).
enforcement: "blocking"  — the rule PASSES TODAY on every budgeted route, because the
root layout (src/app/layout.tsx) establishes it structurally: `<html lang>`, the metadata
title template, one `<main id="obsah">`, the skip link that targets it. So a red here is
a regression THIS change introduced, and it fails `npm run test:e2e` — the
`E2E smoke (Playwright, key-free)` job that .github/required-checks.json names as a check
that may stop a change.
enforcement: "reporting" — the rule COUNTS findings and nothing here has ever measured
them, so `baseline` is null and a count fails nothing. Every run attaches its counts to
the Playwright report and annotates them, which is exactly what a first ratchet needs.
Promoting one is the same two-part diff as every threshold in this repository: the
measured number, and the reason it is now the ceiling. Never raise a baseline you could
have lowered by fixing the finding (rubric B3).
WHAT IS MEASURED, stated so a green line is not over-read. The page is loaded, the run waits
until the streamed `<main>` has replaced the Suspense fallback, and the DOM is then queried
ONCE. That means the assertions are about the settled document — the same thing a screen
reader would walk — and not about the shell. The root layout's fallback is a placeholder
`<main aria-hidden>`, so waiting for a main that is NOT aria-hidden is what makes 'exactly
one <main>' a statement about the page rather than a race with the stream. `networkidle`
would be the intuitive wait and it is the wrong one here: `next dev` keeps talking to the
browser, and a gate that fails on a bundler's chatter teaches people to re-run the build.
WHERE IT RUNS. tests/a11y-budget.spec.ts, inside `npm run test:e2e`. The registry's own
shape is held on every build by test-unit/a11y-budget.test.mjs (blocking, inside
`npm run test:unit` → `check:ci` → .husky/pre-push), because a budget naming a route that
no longer exists checks nothing and says so to nobody.

metric.waitUntil: load, then a <main> that is not the aria-hidden Suspense fallback
metric.why: The DOM a screen reader and a keyboard actually walk, after the streamed shell has been replaced by the real page. Asserting against the shell would be asserting against Suspense fallbacks.

notCovered: Colour contrast. It needs computed backgrounds resolved through the token cascade and a WCAG contrast implementation; docs/design-system.md owns the tokens and the design specs cover the palette. A wrong answer here would be worse than none.
Screen-reader semantics beyond the accessible NAME — reading order, live-region politeness, table header association. Those need an accessibility tree, which is a different instrument.
Motion and vestibular safety. `prefers-reduced-motion` handling for the framer-motion surfaces is a design review, not a DOM query.
Zoom reflow at 400% and pointer-target size. Both need viewport manipulation and a layout oracle this budget does not have.
The authed product at /app. Every route below is key-free and account-free; the authed shell is covered by tests/first-run.spec.ts for behaviour and by nothing for accessibility yet.
Anything a rule below does not name. This is a floor with six blocking invariants and six counted ones, not an audit — do not read a green run as 'this page is accessible'.

rules.label: the document declares a language
rules.why: Without `lang` a screen reader pronounces Czech with an English voice and a translation layer guesses. The root layout sets `lang="en"` statically and a before-paint script upgrades it to `cs` from the locale cookie, so an empty value means one of those two broke.

rules.label: the document has a title
rules.why: The title is the first thing a screen reader announces on navigation and the only label a tab, a bookmark and a history entry get. The metadata template in src/app/layout.tsx guarantees one, so an empty title means a route exported metadata that overrode it away.

rules.label: exactly one main landmark
rules.why: `<main>` is the target of every 'skip to content' affordance the browser and the assistive technology provide. The root layout renders exactly one; zero means the chrome swallowed it, and two means a page nested its own — both leave the landmark navigation ambiguous.

rules.label: the skip link resolves
rules.why: A keyboard user tabbing into a page with a full navigation pays for every link in it before reaching the content. The layout's `<a href="#obsah">` is the way out and it is only a way out while `#obsah` still exists — renaming the main's id is a one-word diff that silently strands it.

rules.label: no positive tabindex
rules.why: A `tabindex` above zero moves an element to the FRONT of the whole document's tab order, ahead of the skip link. This tree uses only 0 and -1 (roving tab stops in AiAssistant, CommandPalette, AppSidebar and Modal), so the first positive one is a decision somebody should have to defend.

rules.label: pinch zoom is not disabled
rules.why: `user-scalable=no` or a `maximum-scale` under 2 stops a low-vision user magnifying the page on a phone, and it is the single most common accessibility regression a copy-pasted viewport meta introduces. The `viewport` export in src/app/layout.tsx sets neither.

rules.label: images carry alt text
rules.why: An `` with no `alt` attribute at all is announced by its filename. An empty `alt=""` is a valid and deliberate answer (decoration) and is NOT counted here — only the missing attribute is, because that is the one nobody chose.

rules.label: interactive controls have an accessible name
rules.why: An icon-only button with no `aria-label` is announced as 'button'. This is where a design system that leans on iconography loses a keyboard user, and it is the finding an agent adding one more toolbar button is most likely to introduce.

rules.label: form controls are labelled
rules.why: A `<label for>`, a wrapping label, `aria-label` or `aria-labelledby` — any of them. A placeholder is not a label: it disappears the moment the field has a value, which is exactly when a user re-checks what they are filling in.

rules.label: one h1, and no skipped heading levels
rules.why: Headings are how a screen reader user skims. Two h1s make the outline ambiguous and an h2→h4 jump makes a section look nested under something it is not — both are what happens when a component is moved between pages.

rules.label: link text says where it goes
rules.why: Assistive technology can list a page's links out of context, where 'click here', 'zde' and 'more' identify nothing. Bilingual on purpose: cs is the home-market locale and the same filler exists on both sides.

rules.label: in-page anchors resolve
rules.why: A `href="#id"` pointing at nothing does not move focus, so a table of contents becomes a set of controls that appear to do nothing. tests/clanek-anchors.spec.ts covers the article pages; this counts the same failure everywhere else.

routes.label: Homepage
routes.why: The marketing entry point and the most-linked page in the product — the page a visitor arriving from anywhere lands on, and the one where the skip link and the landmark structure are load-bearing because the navigation above them is long.

routes.label: Demo app shell — portfolio overview
routes.why: The product's shop window and the heaviest composition on the public side: charts, stat tiles and icon-dense controls, which is exactly the family of markup where an accessible name goes missing.

routes.label: Campaign triage
routes.why: A dense table surface with row-level actions (src/lib/a11y/rowActivation.ts exists because of it). Tables and roving tab stops are where keyboard reachability breaks first.

routes.label: Winning-patterns library
routes.why: A filter-and-cards surface: the page most likely to grow a control that is reachable by mouse and by nothing else.

routes.label: Free channels
routes.why: The seeded free-channel plan — a long list of headed sections, which makes it the page where a heading-order regression is both most likely and least visible.
